newsitem.title: USA: Leon County, Fla., tax notes affected by COPs rule.
newsitem.headline: Leon County, Fla., tax notes affected by COPs rule.

text.p: Tax collectors in Florida's Leon County are in a quandry over how to handle tax certificates sold against ad valorem revenues that a court has prevented the county from collecting.
The county sold about $400,000 of tax certificates against back taxes it expected to collect from the Leon County Educational Facilities Authority for a college dormitory project the authority owned.
The authority believed the property to be exempt from local taxation under Florida law, which exempts "property owned and used by" governmental units.

But the Leon County property appraiser and two lower courts held that the property was taxable because the authority did not hold legal title to the property. The project was financed with certificates of participation and the title was vested in the financing entity, SRH Inc.
The authority appealed to the Florida Supreme Court, which ruled last week that the property was exempt from ad valorem taxes because it served "an essential public function."
That leaves the county wondering what to do with the certificates.
"This has never happened before to my knowledge," Deputy Leon County Tax Collector Ken Mayo said Wednesday.
Mayo said the holders of the tax certificates would get back their money.
"The question is, where do they get it from? Does that come from the county, the school, the taxing authority?" Mayo said.
The tax collector has asked legal counsel to review that question, as well as to advise the county how the interest should be handled. The certificates carried an interest rate of about 8 percent.
"The question there is, who pays the interest back to the certificate holder," Mayo said. "The law would not allow us, if we cancelled the certificates, to pay those rates."
Mayo said a decision on how to handle the certificates was expected within a few weeks.
